paraphrases.note: disciplinary 强调纪律管理；code of conduct 强调行为规范。
take part in 强调参加活动，become a member 强调成员身份。
progress 强调进步过程，results 强调成绩。

sentences.pattern: What makes + aspect of school + valuable is + noun phrase.
sentences.cn: 使校园生活中某方面有价值的是……。
sentences.example: What makes group projects valuable is the need to negotiate with classmates.

sentences.pattern: It was not until + time/event + that + subject + realised + clause.
sentences.cn: 直到某个时间或事件之后，某人才意识到……。
sentences.example: It was not until my final year that I realised how much I had learned outside lessons.

sentences.pattern: Provided that + condition, + school practice + can + benefit.
sentences.cn: 只要满足某个条件，某种学校做法就能……。
sentences.example: Provided that rules are explained consistently, school discipline can create a fairer environment.

expressions.example: It took me a few weeks to settle into my new school.
I got on with most of my classmates, even though we had different interests.
A long absence can make pupils fall behind with schoolwork.
Taking part in extracurricular activities helped me become more confident.
Shared traditions can create a sense of belonging among pupils.

mistakes.wrong: I studied in a boarding school for three years ago.
mistakes.correct: I studied at a boarding school three years ago.
mistakes.why: 表示学校地点用 at；明确的过去时间不能和 for 连用。

mistakes.wrong: The teacher gave us many homeworks.
mistakes.correct: The teacher gave us a lot of homework.

mistakes.wrong: I joined in the school basketball club.
mistakes.correct: I joined the school basketball club.
mistakes.why: 表示成为组织成员时，join 后直接接组织。

writingIdeas.viewpoint: Extracurricular activities are an essential part of school life.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: Schools should protect time for activities that develop abilities beyond examination performance.
writingIdeas.argument: Clubs, sports and performances require pupils to cooperate in situations that ordinary lessons rarely provide. Through these activities, young people can discover strengths that are not measured by written tests. A quiet pupil, for instance, may become an effective organiser during a school production. Participation can also connect students from different classes and reduce isolation. Extracurricular provision should therefore be treated as part of education rather than an optional reward.

writingIdeas.viewpoint: School rules work best when pupils understand their purpose.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: Discipline is more effective when rules are limited, consistent and clearly justified.
writingIdeas.argument: Rules can protect learning time and prevent stronger pupils from intimidating others. However, unexplained restrictions may be viewed as arbitrary and encourage resistance rather than responsibility. Schools should state which harm each rule is intended to prevent and apply consequences consistently. Inviting pupils to discuss implementation can reveal practical problems without giving them control over every decision. This approach teaches that authority should be accountable as well as firm.

speaking.question: What did you enjoy most about your school days?
speaking.answer: I enjoyed the ordinary time between lessons more than any formal event. My friends and I would sit near the sports field, share snacks and talk about whatever had happened that morning. Those short breaks made a fairly demanding school day feel much lighter. I still remember the atmosphere more clearly than most of the classes.

speaking.question: Describe a memorable event at your school.
speaking.answer: I would like to describe a science exhibition held during my final year. Each class had to demonstrate an idea to younger pupils, and my group built a simple water filter from sand, charcoal and recycled bottles. The first version leaked badly, so we spent several afternoons improving it. On the day, children kept asking thoughtful questions, which made the work feel worthwhile. I remember it because it was one of the few school tasks where solving a practical problem mattered more than earning a mark. We displayed the filter beside samples of clean and muddy water, and visitors could pour water through it themselves. Our teacher stayed in the background, so we had to divide the explanations and deal with unexpected questions. By the end, I was tired of repeating the basic steps but proud that the younger pupils remained curious.

reading.title: The Unwritten Curriculum of the School Day
paragraphs: A timetable presents school as a sequence of lessons, but pupils also learn during queues, lunch breaks and journeys between classrooms. In these less supervised moments, they decide who may join a game, how to respond to an insult and whether a rule still matters when no adult is watching. Education researchers sometimes call this the hidden curriculum: the social expectations communicated through routines and relationships rather than through an official syllabus.

The hidden curriculum can support formal teaching. A school that gives pupils genuine responsibility for equipment or events allows them to practise reliability. Mixed-age activities may enable older students to guide younger ones, turning patience into a visible norm. Such experiences are difficult to reproduce in a worksheet. They also provide evidence of abilities—negotiation, initiative and self-control—that conventional examinations record poorly.

However, informal learning is not automatically positive. Status can be distributed according to wealth, athletic ability or confidence, leaving some pupils repeatedly excluded. Rules may also carry unintended messages. If teachers demand punctuality but frequently arrive late, or invite discussion but punish respectful disagreement, students learn that authority is exempt from its own principles. The lesson absorbed may be more powerful than the one stated in an assembly.

Since the 1990s, many schools have used pupil councils and peer-support programmes to make social learning more deliberate. Their success depends less on having a committee than on whether students influence decisions of suitable scale. Choosing a charity event is meaningful; pretending that pupils control staffing is not. Adults remain responsible for safety, yet they can explain limits honestly and model the conduct they expect. Seen in this light, school life is not simply the background to academic education. It is one of the main places where young people test how a community works.

Space contributes to this education too. A shared courtyard can invite cooperation across friendship groups, whereas narrow corridors organised only for movement provide few safe opportunities to pause. School architecture does not determine behaviour, but it quietly shapes which encounters become easy, supervised or avoidable during an ordinary day.
